new_statements.quote: There has not been any opportunity for lab analysis that would have allowed for a definition of the stress. The stressed syllable is marked by pitch, probably together with loudness. In the word, the stress usually falls on the last syllable, for simple and compound words: ŋuni ŋun'ni "village" ... [p. 83:] It is interesting to observe that not all suffixes influence the stress pattern on words in the same way. Indeed, grammatical suffixes of dual and plural cause the word to behave as if it were extended by one syllable – thereby allowing the stress to shift from last syllable in singular to suffix as last syllable in dual and plural ... The suffixation of any conjugation mark, except for the mark of simple past –t, however, fails to bring change in the stress pattern of the verb, even though, technically, one syllable is added to the verb

STRESS PATTERN"), p. 98 = printed 83, p. 99 = printed 84, p. 100 = Chapter II p. 85, so the locator "printed pp. 82-84 = PDF pp. 97-99" is correct. Checked the held page images and -: every quoted sentence is on the page as quoted: "There has not been any opportunity for lab analysis that would have allowed for a definition of the stress. The stressed syllable is marked by pitch, probably together with loudness. In the word, the stress usually falls on the last syllable, for simple and compound words:" followed…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable of simple and compound words (nouns, including compounds; examples show final stress in 2-4 syllable words). Nominal number suffixes (dual -ni, plural -ri?) count as part of the word and take the stress. Verbal conjugation suffixes (present -re, future -rene, perfect -ŋget, etc.) do NOT take stress: the verb keeps stress on the last syllable of the root; the only exception is the simple-past suffix -t, which adds no syllable unless a vowel is inserted (kip 'come' > ki'vat 'he came'), in which case stress moves to the new final syllable. Stress is realised mainly by pitch; the author states no instrumental analysis was possible.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbal inflectional suffixes other than simple past -t are unstressed (stress stays on root-final syllable): ta'ro? 'finish', ta'ro?re 'he finishes', ta'ro?rene 'he will finish'; minimal pairs given: kwa'kre 'chicken' vs 'kwa?re 'he gets out of the way'; vo'ret 'big' vs 'vo?re 'he digs'; 'yembre 'he knows' vs ye'mbat 'he knew'. Also 'ri re? 'garden tool' vs ri're? 'what?' (p. 83). Usher's New Guinea World summary of Levy 2002: 184-190 adds that 1st and 2nd person dual pronouns (both ŋga) 'are said to be distinguished by stress'. Author hedges with 'usually' and notes no lab analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (simple and compound words, including inflected nouns and verbs); examples are isolated words and short noun phrases (kA'ma nde? 'kema's place'), not connected speech. Stress marked by pitch (probably plus loudness).
new_statements.identity_note: Levy 2002 describes the Awar-village variety (Awar village = largest and authoritative; Nubia village variety treated as a dialect with minor segmental variants, e.g. [poyon] vs [pokon], [dz] vs [dj]); this is the language-level glottocode awar1249 itself (no separate Glottolog dialect codes). Older sources (Capell 1951-52) call the language 'Nubia'.
